ai.definition: Digital physics is an interdisciplinary field that investigates the idea that the universe operates on principles similar to those of digital computing, suggesting that all physical phenomena can be described by complex computations.
ai.howItWorks: In digital physics, the universe's fundamental entities and processes are modeled as information-processing systems. This involves representing space-time and quantum mechanics through computational frameworks, potentially leading to new insights into the nature of reality.
ai.problemSolved: Digital physics aims to reconcile classical and quantum mechanics by providing a unified framework for understanding physical phenomena at both macroscopic and microscopic scales.
ai.manufacturing: Not directly involved in manufacturing but could influence future designs and simulations in robotics, AI, and nanotechnology.
ai.buildProcess: Theoretical development involving mathematical modeling and computational simulations rather than physical construction processes.
ai.costDrivers: Primarily driven by research funding, computational resources for simulations, and academic collaboration networks.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: long-term theoretical exploration with potential future applications in computing and physics.
ai.regulation: Not currently regulated as a technology but may influence future regulations on AI and quantum technologies.
ai.risks: Theoretical risks include the inability to validate computational models against real-world phenomena and the philosophical implications of reducing physical reality to computation.
ai.profitability: Indirectly through advancements in related fields like quantum computing, AI, and materials science; not directly profitable as a standalone technology.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential for integration with other theoretical physics concepts such as string theory and quantum gravity, leading to new computational models of the universe.

glossary.def: A field that explores the idea that the universe operates on principles similar to those of digital computing.
Models used in digital physics to represent physical phenomena as computations.

subsystems.name: Discrete substrate
subsystems.role: the hypothetical 'hardware' of reality — a finite set of states rather than continuous fields.

subsystems.name: Update rule
subsystems.role: the 'clock': a local rule that turns one state of the substrate into the next.

subsystems.name: Emergence layer
subsystems.role: the mathematics that would recover continuous space, time and quantum mechanics from the discrete rule.

subsystems.name: Information accounting
subsystems.role: tests whether a proposed substrate holds the right amount of information.

subsystems.name: Quantum simulation tools
subsystems.role: hardware used to run candidate rules that no classical computer can handle.
parts: trapped ions, neutral atoms, superconducting qubits

subsystems.name: Discreteness probes
subsystems.role: instruments looking for any measurable graininess in space-time.

buildSteps.title: Pick a substrate
buildSteps.detail: Choose the fundamental objects: bits or qubits arranged on a lattice, or events linked by causal relations, with a finite state each.

buildSteps.title: Write a local, reversible rule
buildSteps.detail: The rule must depend only on nearby cells and lose no information, so that the model can support the reversible laws of physics we observe.

buildSteps.title: Recover known physics
buildSteps.detail: Show that at distances far larger than the cell size the model reproduces ordinary particles, fields, gravity and the symmetries of special relativity — the hardest step, since a simple lattice tends to single out a preferred frame.

buildSteps.title: Count the information
buildSteps.detail: Compare the model's entropy for a given region with the holographic bound (entropy grows with surface area, not volume). A naive three-dimensional grid stores far too much and is ruled out by black-hole thermodynamics.

buildSteps.title: Simulate small versions
buildSteps.detail: Run tiny lattices on classical supercomputers and on quantum processors, measuring entanglement growth and whether the simulated physics looks like ours.

buildSteps.title: Search for graininess
buildSteps.detail: If space-time is discrete at the Planck scale (about 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ m, or 5.4 × 10⁻⁴⁴ s), light of different energies might travel at very slightly different speeds over cosmological distances, and interference patterns might blur. Observatories already test this.

buildSteps.title: Constrain or confirm
buildSteps.detail: Each null result lowers the maximum allowed cell size; a confirmed signal would be the first direct evidence that physics is computational.

prerequisites.why: gives the language of qubits, entanglement and information bounds in which these models are written.
candidate rules are exponentially hard for classical machines; today's quantum devices are still small and noisy.
current precision measurements set the limits any discrete model must respect, and are the main way to look for a grain in space-time.
they constrain how much information a region may contain, but a full derivation from an underlying discrete theory is missing.

prerequisites.tech: A working theory of quantum gravity
prerequisites.why: without it there is no agreed way to combine the discrete hypothesis with gravity and curved space-time.

pathway.milestone: discrete and information-based models of physics studied as mathematics, with no experimental evidence for a digital substrate
pathway.unlocks: a shared language — information, entropy and computation — across quantum theory, gravity and thermodynamics.

pathway.milestone: quantum simulators running larger, longer-lived lattice and cellular-automaton models
pathway.unlocks: the ability to test whether a simple local rule can produce rich, stable, realistic physics.

pathway.milestone: tighter limits from cosmic photon timing and precision interferometry, or a first positive signal of discreteness
pathway.unlocks: either a decisive push toward the Planck scale, or strong grounds to abandon naive discrete models.

pathway.milestone: a discrete model that predicts something new and is then confirmed
pathway.unlocks: physics rebuilt on an informational foundation — with the concept remaining, more likely, a powerful mathematical lens rather than a proven description of reality.
